lesson.title: From Allies to Adversaries: How the Cold War Began
lesson.summary: The wartime alliance between the United States and the Soviet Union collapsed within months of victory, as ideological differences, competing visions for Europe, and mutual distrust hardened into decades of global rivalry.
lesson.body:
During World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union had been allies out of necessity, united by a common enemy in Nazi Germany, but the partnership rested on almost nothing else. The United States was a capitalist democracy; the Soviet Union was a one party communist state built by Joseph Stalin through purges, forced collectivization, and the deaths of millions of his own citizens. At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin had papered over their disagreements about the future of Europe, agreeing in vague terms that liberated nations like Poland would hold free elections. Stalin had no real intention of honoring that promise in any country his Red Army occupied.

By the time the Allies met again at Potsdam in July and August 1945, the alliance was fraying badly. Roosevelt was dead, replaced by a far less trusting Harry Truman, and the Red Army already controlled most of Eastern Europe, installing communist governments in Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary in the months that followed. Truman also arrived at Potsdam having just learned of the successful test of the atomic bomb, and he mentioned the weapon to Stalin, who, thanks to Soviet spies, already knew more about the bomb than Truman realized. The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on August 6 and August 9, 1945, ended the war with Japan, but they also gave the United States a temporary monopoly on the most destructive weapon ever built, a fact that deeply alarmed Stalin and shaped Soviet strategy for years afterward.

Both sides had reasons, from their own perspective, to feel threatened. The Soviet Union had lost an estimated twenty million people in the war and had been invaded from the west twice in the twentieth century; Stalin wanted a buffer of friendly, controlled states in Eastern Europe to prevent a third invasion. The United States, having just helped build the United Nations on principles of self-determination and open elections, saw Soviet domination of Eastern Europe as a betrayal of the Yalta promises and a dangerous replay of the totalitarian expansion the war had just been fought to stop. Winston Churchill captured the growing Western alarm in a speech delivered in Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946, warning that "an iron curtain has descended across the Continent," dividing a free Western Europe from a Soviet dominated East.

American diplomats were reaching similar conclusions. George Kennan, a State Department official stationed in Moscow, sent an eight thousand word cable back to Washington in February 1946, known as the Long Telegram, arguing that Soviet hostility grew out of both Marxist ideology and traditional Russian insecurity, and that it could not be resolved through negotiation or friendship. Kennan's analysis, along with the slow withdrawal of Soviet troops from northern Iran and Soviet pressure on Turkey over control of the straits leading to the Mediterranean, convinced American policymakers that the wartime alliance was over and that a new, long, tense standoff between two rival superpowers, soon called the Cold War, had begun.
